newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: VERPLAETSE AT BIS TO TACKLE EMU, NEW WORLD ORDER.
newsitem.headline: VERPLAETSE AT BIS TO TACKLE EMU, NEW WORLD ORDER.

text.p: The transformation of European central banking and the new economic world order will be the key challenges facing Alfons Verplaetse when he takes over as President of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).

Verplaetse, governor of the Belgian National Bank (BNB), was on Monday elected by the board of the BIS to succeed Dutch central bank president Wim Duisenberg, who on July 1 takes over the helm of the European Monetary Institute (EMI), the forerunner of the European Central Bank (ECB).
The public profile of the BIS presidency is low, but among central bankers the job is prestigous.

The BIS, the world's oldest international financial institution, has a unique standing among international organisations, such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) or the OECD, because it is owned and governed by central banks.
Its central function is to serve as a forum for cooperation among central banks, but the BIS also provides banking services, including financing for countries facing sudden emergencies.
During a liquidity crises at one of its members, the BIS president has to act fast and rely on the implicit support of his board in drawing on the BIS' financing facilities.
"The BIS president has to act wisely from a banking point of view," said one senior European central banker, noting many of these short-term loans are never known to the public.

Over the years -- notably in the British sterling crises of the 1960s -- the BIS participated in ad hoc assistance to defend speculative attacks on currencies and it was also active in arranging a $10 billion line of credit to Mexico in 1995.
But the real challenges facing Verplaetse will be to adapt the BIS, traditionally a European-dominated institution, to the new economic world order to assure its future role and legitimacy.
Under the two-term stewardship of Duisenberg, the BIS took the first critical steps in expanding its global presence and it will be up to Verplaetse to continue this process.
Last year the BIS expanded its membership with nine new central banks, symbolising its intention to play a key role in the world's future power structure, gradually shifting to the East.
The nine central banks joining the BIS are from Russia, China, India, Hong Kong, Singapore, South Korea, Saudi Arabia, Brazil and Mexico. It brings BIS' membership to 41 central banks.
It is too early to tell whether Verplaetse will take new initiatives to expand its membership, but it is clear that the BIS' global ambition is far from over.
"The BIS started by expanding its membership, but this is not the final word," said one informed source.

With a membership spanning the globe, the BIS will have to decide whether to extend its opening hours so it can provide around-the-clock services. Another issue is whether it should open offices in other parts of the world and even hold meetings away from its tower-like headquarter in the Swiss city of Basle.
A second challenge facing Verplaetse is the transformation of European central banking under a single currency.
If Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) starts on schedule in 1999, many of Europe's sovereign central banks, will be reduced to regional branches of a central European bank.
"There are a lot of governors on the board, who no longer will be real governors," said one senior central banker.

Since 1994, the BIS's board of directors has been identical with the Group of 10 (G10) industrial nations. Prior to 1994, when the U.S., Japan and Canada took up their seats on the BIS board, it was purely a European board.
G10 actually comprises 11 countries: the U.S., Japan, Germany, Canada, France, Britain, Italy, the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden and Switzerland.
The thorny issue of convincing some of Europe's central banks to eventually give up their seats on the BIS board will fully challenge Verplaetse's diplomatic skills.
But Verplaetse and the BIS are far from alone in grappling with this delicate issue because the G10 must also find a solution.
"How will the G10 maintain its credibility if Belgium has a seat, but not China or Russia," said one economist.
